source: Written 2026-10-23/24 by Claude Sonnet from our own summaries of the NC 2017 standards, and solved blind by Claude Opus (Claude Code agents, not runAi: no ai_runs rows), code-checked by lintQuestion; "checked" questions await a platform admin.

notes.NC17.K.CC.1: Counting forward only, by ones and tens within 100. Skills: next number by ones (5), next number by tens (7), missing numbers (4), counting across a ten (4), counting up to 100 (3), starting at any number (3), patterns of tens (4).
notes.NC17.K.CC.3: Numerals cannot be drawn or traced in text, so the questions test choosing or writing the right numeral for a number word, a count told in words, and zero as none. Handwriting form (reversed digits) cannot be tested here. Counts are told in words, never shown as a picture.
notes.NC17.K.CC.4: Shapes, dot cards and hands are written out in words; seeing 1-5 at a glance is tested through described dot patterns (square, triangle, 2+3 split). Numbers stay within 20 and every question is one step.
notes.NC17.K.CC.5: Picture work is written out as rows of letters or lists of names, counted in the text. Counts stay within 20; no question asks how many more, and none chains comparisons. Counting categories (how many of one kind) is left out: it belongs to K.MD.3.
notes.NC17.K.CC.6: Pictures are written out as rows of O. Kindergarten compares only (more, fewer, same), never how much more; matching questions are one step.
notes.NC17.K.CC.7: Only two written numerals are compared at a time, all within 1 to 10; no question asks how much more or less, and none chains comparisons. Comparison words are greater than, less than and equal to; the symbols are left to Grade 1.
notes.NC17.K.G.1: Kindergarten: shapes and positions are given in words only. A ball is called a sphere; shapes are named, never counted by sides beyond what the standard needs. Some questions list items by name so the student must know which are spheres, cylinders, cubes or circles. No pictures.
notes.NC17.K.G.2: Kindergarten: shapes are named from sides, corners, faces or everyday things written out, since no pictures are shown. Naming is a choice skill by nature, so only 7 numeric questions are written: each counts the shapes (or things) that have one name, which needs the naming first. Names used: circle, square, triangle, rectangle, hexagon, sphere, cube, cone, cylinder. Descriptions of a square never list rectangle among the options, because a square is also a rectangle. Orientation and size appear in the turned-shape and big/small questions.
notes.NC17.K.G.3: Only flat-or-solid is tested (naming shapes and their attributes belong to other standards). Pictures are written out, so everyday objects (ball, box, can) stand for solid shapes and a drawing on paper for a flat one. A few numeric questions give the position in a written list.
notes.NC17.K.G.4: Thirty questions in words only (no pictures): same shape in different sizes and turns, flat against solid, corners and sides, and sorting short lists. Comparisons are never "how many more".
notes.NC17.K.G.6: Shapes are written out in words; no pictures. Kindergarten counts stay within 10 and each question is one step.
notes.NC17.K.MD.1: Words only, so the questions ask which words and things are measurable and which attribute a word tells about (length, height, weight). No comparing and no "how much more" (that is K.MD.2). 9 of 30 are numeric because only counting questions ("how many of these words...") fit a number answer; the rest are choice. Skills: tell what can be measured (6), match a word to its attribute (6), choose what to measure (7), name several attributes of one object (7), pick an object that has an attribute (4).
notes.NC17.K.MD.2: Kindergarten compares two objects directly and never asks how much more, so every question asks which one, or counts objects against one reference object (each compared directly, never chained). Pictures are written out in words; numeric questions are counts or a typed object number (1 or 2). Only length, height and weight are used, with line-up-the-ends and the attribute word.
notes.NC17.K.MD.3: Kindergarten: lists are written out as words; counts kept within 12 and no question asks how many more. Sorting is by color, shape, size or kind.
notes.NC17.K.NBT.1: All pictures (ten frames, strips, bundles) are described in words. No question asks how much more; compare questions ask only who has more.
notes.NC17.K.OA.1: Representations (fingers, drawings, acting out) are written as short stories; everything within 10.
notes.NC17.K.OA.2: Everything is one step and inside 10. Skills: add to (6), take from (6), put together (6), take apart / one part unknown (6), matching a story and a number sentence (6). The change-unknown and start-unknown problems are Grade 1 (OA.1), so they are left out. Objects and drawings are written as a story (blocks, circles Zoe draws).
notes.NC17.K.OA.3: Zero is left out as a part (Kindergarten pairs here use 1 or more in each part). Drawings are replaced by number sentences and short stories. Order of a pair (3 and 4 versus 4 and 3) is never asked, since it is ambiguous at this age.
notes.NC17.K.OA.4: Written for Kindergarten: one step, numbers 0 to 10, ten-frames and objects described in words. Skills: story 7, number sentence 4 (+ missing start 3), ten-frame 3, pairs 6, zero and ten 3.
notes.NC17.K.OA.5: Kept to sums and differences within 5, one step, no missing-number sentences (those come in Grade 1). Pictures are told in words.
notes.NC17.K.OA.6: Total up to 5, one step. "Without counting one by one" (subitizing) cannot be tested in text, so groups are written as numbers and the questions test combining small groups and their partners.

questions.skill: Add pieces to a larger shape
questions.stem: A rectangle has 5 squares in a row. Joel puts another row of 5 squares under it to make a bigger rectangle. How many squares are in the bigger rectangle?
questions.solution: The first row has 5 squares and the new row has 5 squares: 5 + 5 = 10.
